title: AP Cybersecurity
summary: Practise defensive risk analysis, access control and evidence-based detection across five units.
frameworkNote: Checked against the new five-unit 2026-27 course on 15 October 2026. All scenarios are fictional defensive exercises. They require no probing, credential collection or changes to real systems. Text practice does not replace supervised labs, authorised hands-on work or required course assessments.

modules.title: Separate identity, authentication and risk
modules.focus: Unit 1: recognise social engineering and choose layered controls.
explanation: Identification names a claimed identity; authentication checks evidence supporting that claim; authorisation determines what the verified identity may do. A strong login alone does not justify unrestricted access. Risk combines the likelihood and impact of a threat acting on a vulnerability.

Social engineering exploits trust, urgency or authority. A message’s familiar display name is not sufficient proof of origin. Use an independently known channel to verify unusual requests, report suspicious messages through approved processes and avoid sharing credentials. Multiple factors should come from different factor categories rather than two versions of the same secret.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional message asks a student to send a password immediately to avoid account closure.
steps: Identify urgency and a request for a secret as warning signs.
Do not reply with credentials; verify through the school’s known support route and report the message.

misconception.claim: Two passwords are two independent authentication factors.
misconception.correction: They are both knowledge factors; a second factor should use a different category.

questions.prompt: Which is authorisation: checking a login code or deciding whether a user may edit records?
questions.answer: Deciding whether the user may edit records is authorisation.

questions.prompt: Why use a known support address instead of the message’s link?
questions.answer: The message may supply an attacker-controlled destination; an independently known route avoids trusting that instruction.

modules.title: Protect spaces without overclaiming certainty
modules.focus: Unit 2: connect physical controls to threats and evidence.
explanation: Physical security protects people, equipment and information through access arrangements, environmental safeguards and monitoring. A locked room, visitor procedure and equipment inventory address different risks. Choose controls for a defined threat rather than collecting devices without a purpose.

Detection evidence requires interpretation. An access log records an event associated with a credential, not necessarily the identity of the person who used it. A missing asset may indicate theft, an undocumented move or an inventory error. Preserve records and follow the authorised reporting process before drawing conclusions.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional lab has an unlogged visitor and a missing laptop.
steps: Record the known facts and preserve relevant inventory and access records.
Report through the designated process and compare authorised moves before asserting who removed the device.

misconception.claim: An access-card event proves the named person was physically present.
misconception.correction: A credential may be shared, lost or misused; corroboration is needed.

questions.prompt: What risk does a visitor sign-in process address?
questions.hint: Think about accountability and permitted access.
questions.answer: It helps establish who was authorised to enter and when, supporting access control and later review.
It provides a baseline for detecting missing or moved equipment and distinguishing documented changes from unexplained ones.

modules.title: Reason about segmentation and logs
explanation: Network segmentation separates groups of devices so that access can be controlled between them. A guest network should not automatically reach sensitive administrative systems. A firewall rule describes permitted or blocked traffic using defined criteria; its effectiveness depends on placement and the complete rule set.

Logs can reveal unusual patterns, but an alert is not proof of compromise. Compare source, destination, time and expected activity, then preserve the evidence for authorised review. These exercises use fictional descriptions only and do not require scanning or contacting any real network.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional school guest network can reach a records server it does not need.
steps: Identify the unnecessary path and the sensitive asset.
Propose a reviewed rule that blocks guest-to-records access while preserving required services, then verify it in an authorised test environment.

misconception.claim: A firewall makes every device behind it trustworthy.
misconception.correction: Allowed traffic and compromised internal devices still require layered controls.

questions.prompt: Why separate guest devices from administrative systems?
questions.hint: Consider unnecessary access and the impact of compromise.
questions.answer: Separation limits paths that guest devices do not need and can reduce the reach of an incident.
checkpoints: Does not promise total isolation without verification

questions.prompt: A log shows repeated denied connections. Does that prove a successful breach?
questions.answer: No. It shows denied activity; investigation must determine its source, context and whether any access succeeded.

modules.title: Use a device baseline and safe response
modules.focus: Unit 4: manage updates, permissions and suspicious changes.
explanation: A secure device baseline records expected software, configuration and permitted access. Updates address known defects, while least privilege limits what ordinary accounts can change. Anti-malware tools add detection and prevention but cannot guarantee that every threat is found.

When a device behaves unexpectedly, preserve relevant information and follow the organisation’s response procedure. Unplanned deletion or repeated restarting can destroy useful evidence or complicate recovery. Distinguish a suspicious change from a confirmed compromise and escalate through the authorised support process.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional managed laptop displays an unfamiliar administrator account.
steps: Compare the account with the approved baseline and recent authorised support work.
Report the unexplained difference and follow the response procedure; do not assume a user’s name proves responsibility.

misconception.claim: A clean anti-malware scan proves a device is uncompromised.
misconception.correction: A scan has a detection scope and may miss unknown or hidden activity.

questions.hint: Consider the effect of mistakes or malicious software.
questions.answer: Least privilege limits the changes a normal session can make, reducing potential impact.
checkpoints: Does not claim all threats are prevented

questions.prompt: What should accompany a report of suspicious behaviour?
questions.answer: The time, observed symptoms and relevant error or alert details, without altering or publicly exposing sensitive records.

modules.title: Protect data and interpret access evidence
modules.focus: Unit 5: distinguish encryption, hashing and permission checks.
explanation: Encryption protects confidentiality by making data unreadable without the appropriate key. Hashing produces a digest useful for integrity checks and other constructions, but it does not provide reversible secrecy. Access controls decide which identities may read or change a resource and must be enforced at the relevant system boundary.

A safe review checks whether permissions match roles and whether logs record meaningful events. An unexpected access attempt may be an error or misuse; inspect context before concluding. Backups support recovery only when restoration has been tested under authorised procedures.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional class portal lets one learner request another learner’s private feedback.
steps: Identify an authorisation failure: the requested record belongs to a different user.
Require a server-side ownership or role check for each request and verify it with authorised test accounts; hiding the button alone is insufficient.

misconception.claim: Encrypting data removes the need for access controls.
misconception.correction: An authorised application can decrypt data, so it must still decide which user may receive it.

questions.prompt: Why is a hash not a substitute for encryption when secrecy and recovery are required?
questions.answer: A hash is not designed to recover the original data; encryption supports recovery with a key while protecting confidentiality.

questions.hint: A stored copy alone is not the final outcome.
questions.answer: Testing checks whether the data and required configuration can actually be recovered in a usable form.
checkpoints: Does not assume success from file presence
